To argue that aesthetic value cannot be reduced to purely subjective preference or individual psychological response, we must first look at the very structure of how we experience art and beauty. When a person encounters a profoundly moving work of art and judges it to be beautiful, they do not experience this feeling as a mere personal quirk, like a preference for vanilla ice cream over chocolate. Instead, the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience involves an implicit claim to intersubjective validity. In making an aesthetic judgment, an individual speaks not just for themselves but with what Immanuel Kant described as a universal voice, calling upon others to share in the same appreciation. This normative dimension means that we feel a sense of rightness about a correct aesthetic response and a sense of friction when someone else treats a masterpiece with indifference. A purely subjectivist framework, which treats all aesthetic reactions as isolated psychological events, lacks the conceptual machinery to explain this demanding nature of aesthetic judgments, reducing our shared cultural conversations to a series of disconnected, non-overlapping expressions of personal taste.

This claim to a shared standard becomes even more evident when we examine the actual practice of aesthetic criticism. Criticism is not a collection of arbitrary autobiographical reports; it is an argumentative discipline built on an apparatus of reasons, standards, and education. When a critic analyzes a painting or a novel, they point to specific formal properties, historical contexts, and structural harmonies to justify their evaluation. This entire enterprise presupposes that aesthetic assessments are answerable to considerations that exist independently of individual psychological responses, meaning that a work of art possesses features that actively merit a particular kind of attention. Furthermore, the existence of critical discourse implies that some responses are genuinely better-informed, more perceptive, and more deeply realized than others. If aesthetics were entirely subjective, the concept of cultivation or education in taste would be meaningless, as there would be no objective depth in the object for a viewer to become more sensitive toward over time.

Finally, abandoning these external standards in favor of aesthetic relativism collapses under its own logical weight by generating an inescapable regress. If a relativist asserts that all aesthetic preferences are equally valid because no mind-independent standards exist, they undermine the ground they stand on. Under this logic, the preference for an open, pluralistic, and tolerant view of art is itself nothing more than an individual psychological preference. Consequently, the relativist cannot claim that their pluralism is a better, truer, or more enlightened stance than rigid dogmatism or elitism. By reducing all judgments to mere taste, the relativist strips their own position of any normative force, rendering the argument for relativism an arbitrary whim that can be dismissed just as easily as it was asserted. Therefore, to maintain a coherent understanding of our aesthetic lives, criticism, and philosophical positions, we must acknowledge that aesthetic value points to a reality beyond individual psychology.
